{{Short description|Concept in topology}}
{{Refimprove|date=August 2020}}
{{about|the relation between two sets|the description a single set|Closed set{{!}}Closedness}}

'''Closeness''' is a basic concept in [[topology]] and related areas in [[mathematics]]. Intuitively, we say two sets are close if they are arbitrarily near to each other. The concept can be defined naturally in a [[metric space]] where a notion of distance between elements of the space is defined, but it can be generalized to [[topological spaces]] where we have no concrete way to measure distances.

The [[closure operator]] ''closes'' a given set by mapping it to a [[closed set]] which contains the original set and all points close to it. The concept of closeness is related to [[limit point]].

==Definition==
Given a [[metric space]] <math>(X,d)</math> a point <math>p</math> is called '''close''' or '''near''' to a set <math>A</math> if
:<math>d(p,A) = 0</math>,
where the distance between a point and a set is defined as 
:<math>d(p, A) := \inf_{a \in A} d(p, a)</math>
where inf stands for [[Infimum and supremum|infimum]]. Similarly a set <math>B</math> is called '''close''' to a set  <math>A</math> if
:<math>d(B,A) = 0</math>
where 
:<math>d(B, A) := \inf_{b \in B} d(b, A)</math>.

==Properties==
*if a point <math>p</math> is close to a set <math>A</math> and a set <math>B</math> then <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are close, but the [[Converse (logic)|converse]] is not true.
*closeness between a point and a set is preserved by [[continuous functions]].
*closeness between two sets is preserved by [[uniformly continuous functions]].

==Closeness relation between a point and a set==

Let <math>V</math> be some set. A relation between the points of <math>V</math> and the subsets of <math>V</math> is a closeness relation if it satisfies the following conditions:

Let <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> be two subsets of <math>V</math> and <math>p</math> a point in <math>V</math>.<ref>[[Alexander Arhangelskii|Arkhangel'skii, A. V.]]; [[Lev Pontryagin|Pontryagin, L.S.]] General Topology I: Basic Concepts and Constructions, Dimension Theory. Encyclopaedia of Mathematical Sciences (Book 17), Springer 1990, p. 9.</ref>
*If <math>p \in A</math> then <math>p</math> is close to <math>A</math>.  
*if <math>p</math> is close to <math>A</math> then <math>A \neq \emptyset</math>.
*if <math>p</math> is close to <math>A</math> and <math>B \supset A</math> then <math>p</math> is close to <math>B</math>.
*if <math>p</math> is close to <math>A \cup B</math> then <math>p</math> is close to <math>A</math> or <math>p</math> is close to <math>B</math>.
*if <math>p</math> is close to <math>A</math> and for every point <math>a \in A</math>, <math>a</math> is close to <math>B</math>, then <math>p</math> is close to <math>B</math>.

Topological spaces have a closeness relationship built into them: defining a point <math>p</math> to be close to a subset <math>A</math> if and only if <math>p</math> is in the closure of <math>A</math> satisfies the above conditions. Likewise, given a set with a closeness relation, defining a point <math>p</math> to be in the closure of a subset <math>A</math> if and only if <math>p</math> is close to <math>A</math> satisfies the [[Kuratowski closure axioms]]. Thus, defining a closeness relation on a set is exactly equivalent to defining a topology on that set.

==Closeness relation between two sets==
Let <math>A</math>,<math>B</math> and <math>C</math> be sets.  
*if <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are close then <math>A \neq \emptyset</math> and <math>B \neq \emptyset</math>.
*if <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are close then <math>B</math> and <math>A</math> are close.
*if <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are close and <math>B \subset C</math> then <math>A</math> and <math>C</math> are close.
*if <math>A</math> and <math>B \cup C</math> are close then either <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are close or <math>A</math> and <math>C</math> are close.
*if <math>A \cap B \neq \emptyset</math> then <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are close.

==Generalized definition==
The closeness relation between a set and a point can be generalized to any topological space. Given a topological space and a point <math>p</math>, <math>p</math> is called '''close''' to a set <math>A</math> if <math>p \in \operatorname{cl}(A) = \overline A</math>.

To define a closeness relation between two sets the topological structure is too weak and we have to use a [[uniform structure]]. Given a [[uniform space]], sets <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are called '''close''' to each other if they intersect all [[entourage (topology)|entourages]], that is, for any entourage <math>U</math>, <math>(A\times B)\cap U</math> is non-empty.
